name: Sangameswarar Temple, Bhavani (Thirunana)
deity: Shiva as Sangameswarar, with the goddess Vedanayaki
period: The first Paadal Petra Sthalam of Kongu Nadu, sung by Sambandar in the Tevaram (7th century)
summary: Where the Bhavani joins the Kaveri at Kooduthurai, Shiva reigns as Sangameswarar, Lord of the confluence, in the shrine Sambandar sang as Thirunana — the Triveni of the south.

sections.history: Bhavani stands about 15 km north of Erode, at the point where the river Bhavani, coming down from the Nilgiris, flows into the Kaveri. The temple on the riverbank at Kooduthurai is the Thirunana of the Tevaram: Sambandar sang a pathigam of ten verses to its Lord, gathered in the second Tirumurai, and later Arunagirinathar praised its Murugan in the Tiruppugazh. It is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and is counted first among the seven of Kongu Nadu. The temple also keeps a story from the early nineteenth century, when a British collector at Bhavani, William Garrow, is remembered to have offered the goddess an ivory cradle in thanks for his life.
sections.architecture: The temple stands right beside the meeting of the waters, its bathing ghats stepping down to the rivers at Kooduthurai. Within the walls are the sanctum of Sangameswarar, a separate shrine for the goddess Vedanayaki and a shrine of Murugan. Unusually for a Shiva temple, the complex also holds a shrine of Vishnu as Adikesava Perumal with the goddess Soundaravalli, so that devotees of both traditions worship in one enclosure at the confluence.
sections.legends: Three rivers are said to meet here: the Kaveri and the Bhavani, which can be seen, and the Amudha, a hidden stream of nectar believed to rise from beneath the earth. For this the place is called the Dakshina Triveni Sangamam, the southern counterpart of the confluence at Prayag. Tradition holds that the collector Garrow was warned in a dream to leave his bungalow moments before it fell, and that the ivory gift he made in gratitude still bears his signature.
sections.festivals: Aadi Perukku in July–August, when the rivers run full and families come to offer worship at the confluence, is the temple's great festival. New-moon days, especially Aadi and Thai Amavasai, bring crowds for ancestral rites on the ghats, and Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are kept as well; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: A visit to Bhavani begins at the water. Pilgrims bathe at the Kooduthurai ghats or perform rites for their ancestors where the rivers meet, then climb into the temple to worship Sangameswarar, the goddess Vedanayaki and Adikesava Perumal in turn. At Aadi Perukku the ghats are thronged with families offering lamps and flowers to the swollen Kaveri.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure; the ghats are busiest on new-moon days and at Aadi Perukku. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctums; in the outer corridors and at the ghats, ask before taking pictures and respect families performing rites.
visit.gettingThere: Bhavani is about 15 km north of Erode by road, with frequent town buses from Erode. Erode Junction is the nearest major railway station, and Coimbatore International Airport is the nearest airport, about 100 km away. Take care at the ghats when the rivers are in spate.
